idiom_name: iter.Seq / iter.Seq2 (func(yield func(T) bool)) driven by for ... range
implementation_notes: Go 1.23 standardizes iterators as functions: a container exposes All() iter.Seq[E] and range-over-func lets callers write for v := range c.All(), so the language's own range syntax is the client of the traversal and no Iterator/ConcreteIterator pair exists. iter.Pull converts a push iterator into a pull cursor when a range loop is unnatural (and returns a stop function for early exit), while slices.All, maps.Keys and Collect bridge iterators to the existing slices/maps packages. Choose it for new container APIs on Go 1.23+; keep the classic Next() cursor where older modules must compile.
pitfalls: The yield function's bool must be honoured: an iterator that ignores it keeps computing after a break and skips its cleanup, which range cannot compensate for.
The iterator closure captures the container by reference; mutating the map while ranging it is a race and can panic, and calling the iterator again later observes the new state.

range-over-func requires the module's go directive to be at least 1.23 (or a //go:build go1.23 tag); a pull iterator from iter.Pull must have its stop function called or the underlying push iterator never cleans up.

variants.name: Classic Next() pull cursor
variants.idiom_name: struct with Next() bool + accessor (Value()/Scan(&v)), database/sql Rows style
variants.implementation_notes: Before the iter.Seq standard, the idiomatic Go iterator is a struct with Next() bool plus an accessor - the shape used by database/sql Rows (Next/Scan/Err) and bufio.Scanner (Scan/Text/Bytes). It is a pull cursor: the caller controls the pace, it compiles on any Go version against any module, and it remains the right API when the traversal is a state machine that accumulates an error to report after the loop rather than a pure value sequence. Ranging over a slice of results is still simpler when the data is already materialized.
pitfalls: The accessor is only meaningful after Next() returned true; calling it first or after false silently yields a zero value, so the loop condition is part of the protocol.
The cursor holds mutable traversal state and must be created per traversal; sharing one between goroutines or two loops corrupts the position.
Errors cannot be carried by the protocol, so they accumulate outside it (Err() after the loop, as database/sql does), which is easy to forget - and an early break must still release resources.
